name: libc-search
algorithm: One C kernel (mk/kernel.c) over n bytes from splitmix64 (seed 1), each 1 to 254; pass r writes a NUL at n - 1 - r % 64 and a 255 at n - 2 - r % 64, adds strlen of the buffer and the offset memchr finds for 255 in n bytes, and restores the two bytes; the checksum is the sum over reps passes (README.md).

skip.rust: the row compares C libraries under one C kernel: std.libc against the C runtime; Rust's std has no strlen or memchr of its own a C caller links (memchr is a crate)
skip.zig: the row compares C libraries under one C kernel; Zig's std.mem.indexOfScalar is not what a C source links
skip.go: the row compares C libraries under one C kernel; Go's bytes.IndexByte is not callable from C without cgo
skip.mk-wrap: the kernel is C in both columns; there is no Mk arithmetic to wrap

no_counts: B24 does not apply: the work per pass is fixed by n, and the checksum is each pass's two offsets, which a function that stops early or late changes
notes: What it measures: std.libc's strlen and memchr (Mk, word at a time, as musl's: SQL-11) against the static C runtime's (MSVC ucrt on Windows), called by the same C kernel. The Mk column compiles the kernel as its CSource (-ffreestanding -fno-builtin from the driver, -O3 at --release, -march=x86-64-v2 from pkg.mk) and links std.libc; the C column includes the same file in libc-search.c at -O3 -march=x86-64-v2 and links the C runtime. The kernel writes the buffer on every pass, so no compiler may hoist a call.
std.libc's plan past the word loop is std.simd's 16-byte search when that module has one (status/std-sqlite.md).
